newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria created more jobs in 1995, more seek work.
newsitem.headline: Algeria created more jobs in 1995, more seek work.

text.p: Algeria's economy created 140,000 new jobs in 1995, achieving its best performance after a decade of slump, official figures showed.

But in a sign of the turmoil affecting the economy, the agency said job applications through its office had soared, with an 18 percent hike to 50,000 applicants in the last quarter of 1995 compared with the prior period.

"The total workforce has reached 5,436,000, achieving an increase of 140,000 posts in the past year compared to 1994," said the government-funded National Agency for Employment in a report carried on Monday by the Algerian news agency APS.
More than 48 percent of the job seekers had worked before while 47 percent were newcomers to the market, the agency said.
Youth aged between 16 and 25 years represented 31 percent of the job seekers, it added. Algeria's birthrate is now running at about 2.1 percent after years of more than three percent,

The state-controlled National Office of Statistics estimated the numbers of jobless at 2.1 million in 1995 compared to an estimated 1.52 million unemployed in 1992. Early this month it said 80 percent of the jobless were under 30 years old.

Officials have long said that joblessness, poverty and lack of hope fuelled recruitment to Islamic fundamentalist ranks, whose guerrillas are blamed for sabotage that has cost the economy an estimated $2 billion in the past three years.
An official report said early this year that 10 percent of the industrial capacity was crippled by the strife in which an estimated 50,000 people have been killed.
Algeria's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 4.1 percent in 1995, reversing a fall of 1.8 percent in 1994 and a fall of 2.9 percent in 1993, according to previously released official figures.
Agriculture, which grew 21 percent in 1995 due to good rains and sustained reforms, provided 67,000 new jobs, followed by the services sector with 36,000 jobs, the agency said.
Algeria, the world's largest importer of hard durum wheat, had a record harvest of 4.6 million tonnes of cereals in the 1995/96 season, agriculture ministry figures showed in August.
The previous record was 3.6 million tonnes in 1990/91.
But the report showed that outside farming and Algeria's strong oil and gas sector, industry overall lost 9,000 jobs, underlining its problems trying to switch to a free economy.
Central and local government created 35,000 of the new jobs and the housing and public works sector provided about 10,000.

Excluding oil and gas, which provide more than 90 percent of Algeria's foreign currency income, state industry provides jobs for more than 1.7 million people and produces about 15 percent of the nation's added value, according to experts' estimates.
Last June, the government set up four working groups to try to rescue general state-owned industry from forecast collapse.
Non-energy industry production fell by 2.1 percent in the first quarter of 1996
The government has reported GDP growth of five percent in the first half of 1996.
